biggest_risk: The largest share of your savings sits in your registered account, so once minimum withdrawals from the Registered Retirement Income Fund kick in later in retirement, they could push your taxable income upward year after year whether or not you actually need the cash.
best_lever: Drawing down some of the registered balance during the lower-tax early-retirement years, before mandatory conversion forces the pace, could reshape your lifetime tax bill more than any other single move available to you.
snapshot_intro: Your plan earns the top grade, holding up across nearly every simulated future, which is a genuine win and a strong base to build from. That result reflects thousands of tested scenarios, including severe crashes and prolonged inflation, but it cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative changes, major health issues, or family upheaval. The conversation from here is less about whether the money lasts and more about how hard each dollar could work.
mirror_block: You are a few years from leaving work, with a sizeable nest egg built mostly inside your registered account and topped up by your tax-free savings and a smaller non-registered slice. Government benefits have not started yet, so once you retire there is a brief stretch where your portfolio carries the load before Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security arrive to cover part of your spending. Your home is nearly clear of its mortgage, which means housing costs ease right when retirement begins. The main tension in your file is how much of your wealth lives in one tax-deferred bucket.
revenue_analysis: Your planned retirement spending sits below the income you live on today, which is typical once commuting, saving, and mortgage payments fall away, and it suggests your lifestyle could carry through largely intact. The income structure leans first on guaranteed government benefits and then on portfolio withdrawals to fill the rest, a layering that tends to hold up because the floor is indexed and arrives for life. What matters is that the replacement level you are targeting keeps the texture of your current life rather than forcing a step down.
gov_explanation: Once benefits begin, the guaranteed government floor would cover a meaningful minority of your monthly spending, leaving the portfolio to supply the larger remainder. Before that point, the short bridge between retirement and the start of benefits leans almost entirely on your own savings, which is why the early years and the steady-state years behave like two distinct chapters. Because the floor is indexed and lasts for life, it quietly reduces how hard the portfolio has to work later on, even though it never carries the whole load.
longevity_analysis: Across the simulations, the middle band of outcomes stretches from a cautious lower path to a far more favorable upper one, and roughly half of all tested futures land somewhere inside that range. The cautious end is not a disaster scenario but a reminder that weaker early returns would leave you with a thinner cushion later, while the upper end of the likely range reflects friendlier markets compounding in your favor. The width of that band is mostly a story about when good and bad return years happen to fall.
priority_actions: Your plan already works, so the real question is whether every dollar is working as hard as it could. The fee load you carry is light, yet over a multi-decade horizon even a slim drag compounds into real lost spending, so confirming you are in a genuinely low-cost vehicle keeps more of the growth yours. The richer lever is sequencing: drawing measured amounts from the registered account in the lower-tax window before mandatory conversion, leaning on the tax-free account last, and letting the registered balance shrink before it is forced to, could trim the tax owed across your lifetime and at death. The surplus your plan carries also buys flexibility, meaning a richer travel chapter early on or a larger cushion for health costs could fit without straining the result.
tax_analysis: Your effective tax rate would ease in retirement compared with your working years, simply because withdrawals replace a salary, which gives you a low-tax window in the early retirement years. With the larger part of your savings sitting in the registered account, the forced conversion in your early seventies would start pushing minimum withdrawals into your income whether you spend them or not. Drawing some of that balance down earlier, while your rate is lower, could keep later years from bunching income into a higher bracket.
estate_analysis: Your projected estate would leave a healthy residual in the middle case, with a thinner but still meaningful amount even in the cautious paths. Because your stated preference is to balance lifestyle and legacy rather than maximize either, the structure matters as much as the size: the registered portion would be taxed on the final return while the tax-free portion passes untouched. That contrast is the lever a balanced preference can pull without sacrificing the spending you want in life.
obs_1: **Bridge window** : The short gap between leaving work and the first government cheque leans almost entirely on your own savings, concentrating a self-funded draw into a single early stretch right when sequence risk bites hardest.
obs_2: **Forced-income climb** : Because most of your savings sits in the registered account, the mandatory conversion in your early seventies would steadily lift your taxable income with age, a rising pressure that arrives independent of what you actually choose to spend.
obs_3: **Wealth under one roof** : A large slice of your net worth is locked in your home, and while a sale is already built into the later projection, until then that value cannot be drawn on for monthly needs, so the liquid portfolio carries the early years alone.
obs_4: **Two estates, one number** : The residual you would leave is really two pools with very different tax fates, since the registered balance is taxed on the final return while the tax-free account passes clear, meaning where the money rests matters as much as how much there is.
obs_5: **Floor versus bridge** : Once Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security begin around the standard age, the guaranteed floor would cover a minority of your monthly target, the larger share coming from Canada Pension Plan and the rest from Old Age Security; before they start, the bridge years carry little government support, so the two phases should be read as distinct rather than as one steady coverage level.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years before you retire, while your tax rate is still settling and the registered account has not yet been forced into withdrawals, could be the window where sequencing and fee choices move the needle most. Acting inside that window, rather than waiting until mandatory conversion sets the pace, is where the room to maneuver is widest. The next update of this assessment, in a year, would measure whether those adjustments shifted the trajectory.
model_blind_spots: The simulation does not capture how a deliberate, staged drawdown of the registered account before mandatory conversion might reshape your lifetime tax path, nor does it anticipate life events such as an inheritance, a relationship change, or a shift in health that would redraw the picture. It also assumes the rules governing government benefits stay as they are, when future legislative changes could move both the floor and the conversion timing. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
efficiency_gap: Your plan works. Here is what it could look like if every dollar worked as hard as possible. The fee drag you carry is slim, yet across the full horizon it still quietly subtracts from spendable wealth, and the gap between your working-year tax rate and your retirement rate marks a window where measured registered withdrawals could lower the tax taken over a lifetime. Layer on the registered balance facing full taxation at death versus the tax-free account passing clear, and the difference between the plan that merely survives and one tuned for efficiency is real spending and legacy, not survival.
savings_analysis: Your portfolio is on a rising path into retirement, carried mostly by what you have already built rather than by new contributions, which means the heavy lifting is largely behind you. The accumulation is steady rather than fragile, and the main story now shifts from adding to the pile to deciding how it comes back out. The key takeaway is that the trajectory supports your spending target with room to spare, so the focus moves from growth to structure.
what_if_analysis: Among the alternatives modeled, working a little longer lifts the projected median wealth the most, with delaying Canada Pension Plan to the later age close behind, while saving more barely moves the result. That pattern reveals a plan whose success is already near its ceiling, so the levers that matter are about shaping the timing and the size of the estate rather than rescuing the outcome. In short, your sensitivity is to choices that enrich an already-sound plan, not to ones that keep it afloat.
strategy_comparison: Of the paths compared against staying the course, working longer would leave the largest projected median wealth, with delaying Canada Pension Plan to the later age the next strongest, both edging out the status quo while the success rate barely changes because it is already near the top. Early registered drawdown and saving more land essentially alongside the status quo on wealth. The signal is that the meaningful differences here are about how much is left over, not about whether the plan holds.
fees_analysis: Your investment vehicle is unconfirmed, and the management fee you pay is light by industry standards, yet even a slim rate compounding over decades quietly drains a stretch of retirement income you would otherwise keep. Translated into lifestyle, that cumulative cost amounts to a span of monthly spending forgone across the plan. Confirming you sit in a genuinely low-cost structure is the cheapest way to claw that back.
cpp_timing: Claiming Canada Pension Plan at the earliest age shows a slightly lower success rate than waiting, while claiming at the standard age and deferring to the latest age land essentially together near the top. Deferring trades early years of smaller or no benefit for a larger indexed cheque for life, which tends to matter more the longer one lives. The data lays out the trade-off without pointing to a single right age for you.
spending_flex: Your plan carries built-in flexibility, meaning that in a rough market stretch the modeled spending could dial back by up to a meaningful fraction before recovering, a cushion worth a few hundred dollars a month at its deepest. In the simulations, that brake was never actually triggered, which signals the plan rarely had to lean on it. Spending itself is not flat across retirement either: it tends to step down through the go-go, slow-go, and no-go phases as the pace of life eases.
sequence_risk: Two retirees with identical savings and identical average returns can end up worlds apart depending on the order those returns arrive, because a string of weak years early, while withdrawals are still being taken, permanently shrinks the base that later growth has to work on. That is why the cautious lower path and the far more favorable upper path of your likely range diverge so widely despite starting from the same place. When the parameters are ranked by how much they swing your result, the timing of early returns and your spending level sit near the top of that list.
strengths_risks: Your strengths are concrete: the plan holds across nearly every tested future, your fee load is light, and your home is almost free of its mortgage so housing costs ease as retirement starts. The risks are equally specific: the bulk of your wealth sits in one tax-deferred account that mandatory conversion will eventually force open, your withdrawal rate runs above conventional comfort thresholds in the early years, and a large share of your net worth is tied up in property until a later sale. Strengths give you the room; the risks are about structure and timing, not survival.
